prompt: At one firm, a groupware tool becomes a shared knowledge base; at another, consultants use the same tool only as private email. Over time, each use becomes 'the system' there.
why: Same system, different structures enacted in recurrent use.
trap: It's routine use producing different technologies, not designers' groups debating.

prompt: Years after rollout, a sales team uses only the contact list in their CRM. For them, that habit simply is what the CRM is.
tells: that habit simply is what the CRM is
why: The technology-in-practice is what recurrent use makes it.
trap: The other features still exist; they just aren't enacted.

prompt: On one ward the EHR is used to coordinate care in real time; on another, nurses type everything in at shift end. Researchers call these two different systems in use.
tells: Researchers call these two different systems in use
trap: End-of-shift entry is a routine, not a hidden fix.

prompt: After a reorganization, the same team stops using the tool for status updates and starts using it for code reviews. The study tracks how their enacted structure shifted.
trap: The tool itself doesn't change, so it isn't imbrication.

prompt: Designers built a forecasting tool to encourage collaboration; in daily use, managers use it to monitor staff. The study focuses on what the recurrent use produces, not the designers' intent.
tells: focuses on what the recurrent use produces, not the designers' intent
why: Use, not design intent, constitutes the structure.
trap: The designers' script is the counterpoint, not the lens.

prompt: In one office, the chat tool became where decisions get made; in another, the same tool is only used to book meeting rooms. In each office, that habit is now what the tool is.
tells: In each office, that habit is now what the tool is
why: Recurrent use makes the same system different in practice.
trap: The offices don't coordinate through it, so it isn't a boundary object.
